       1.2 Useful formulas

Let A,B and C be three vector fields and f a scalar field. Let us start this
       small formulary with the following algebraic formula known as the vector
       triple product                                        
                   A ∧ (B ∧ C) = (A · C) B − (A · B) C. (A.3)
       We next have the following formulae which link the various differential oper-
       ators introduced above                                
             div(fA) = f(divA) + (A · ∇)f,        (A.4)

curl(fA) = f(curlA) + (∇f) ∧ A,      (A.5)      
                    1                                        
             (A · ∇)A = ∇|A|2 − A ∧ curlA,        (A.6)      
                    2                                        
           div(A ∧ B) = B · curlA − A · curlB,    (A.7)      
           curl(A ∧ B) = (divB)A − (divA)B + (B · ∇)A − (A · ∇)B, (A.8)
           curl(curlA) = ∇divA − ΔA.              (A.9)      
       Of course, this list is a long way from being exhaustive and only contains the
       formulas which are most useful in fluid mechanics.

Our goal is not to provide a detailed general study of tensors. In this text,
       we only need to consider in detail tensor fields of order 2, that is, the endo-
       morphism fields of Rd.                                
         We therefore simply identify second-order tensors with square matrices via
       the canonical basis of Rd.

         If we apply u ⊗ v to a third vector field w, then we have
                        (u ⊗ v).w = (v · w)u.                
       Furthermore, we have the following formula for the divergence of a tensor
       product                                               
                     div(u ⊗ v) = (divv)u + (v · ∇)u. (A.10) 
         Finally, we can define a scalar product on the set of second-order tensor
       fields, which is simply the Euclidean scalar product in the space of the ma-
       trices identified with Rd×d. In tensor language, this is called the contracted
       tensor product.
